name: Tara Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a big clinic on the edge of a new housing estate, lots of young families and commuters. Half my day is online consultations, where patients send in a form or a photo and I reply or call them back, and the other half is the children's clinic: coughs, rashes, worried first-time parents. I like the kids' clinic, the toddlers who try to steal my stethoscope. What wears me out is the online inbox, which refills faster than I can empty it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you handle that inbox now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: With a lot of AI, honestly. I use the AI scribe all day, and I've set up a tool that sorts the online requests by urgency and drafts replies for the simple ones, which I check and send. I'm on the clinic's digital working group, which mostly means I'm the one people ask when the software breaks. My partner Sam is a nurse on the children's ward at the hospital, so we compare notes on tired parents every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools still save me real time, so I'm not complaining. At work I'd keep pushing the small stuff, like the inbox sorting. Online I'd say the hype hurt the useful bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the money stays tight. Sam and I moved into a rented house this year, and the deposit and furniture wiped out our savings, so we're about three weeks from empty. My pay is on the lower end and there aren't other clinics nearby paying more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using what works and pick up a couple of evening shifts a month for an online doctor service, which pays well per hour. I'd ask the clinic to recognise the digital working group with a bit of extra pay. We'd rebuild some savings over the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, really. A bit tired and a bit broke, but okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Evening shifts on top of a full day. How would that go at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam does nights on the ward sometimes, so we'd try to line my evening shifts up with those. It's not glamorous, but it means we're both working at the same time and both off together. We've done harder rotas than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be disappointed that AI didn't do more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd hoped it would take the inbox off me completely. But I'd still have the sorting tool. An hour back a day is an hour back, even if AI never takes the whole inbox off me.

The **hype** hurt the useful bits, she'd say online.

feel: Okay, if a bit **tired and broke**.
S0.quote: An hour back a day is an hour back, even if AI never takes the whole inbox off me.
fieldNote: The **deposit and furniture** emptied their savings, leaving about three weeks of money.

She's slightly **disappointed** the hype didn't deliver more.

steps.text: Work two evening shifts a month for an online doctor service
Keep using the inbox sorting tool and AI scribe

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for patients if we do it carefully, and I'd help lead it at the clinic. At the working group I'd push for the AI to take the whole online inbox. Online I'd share what worked and what didn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I know my online half is exactly what this takes. Answering patients, checking forms, writing replies: that's the list on the card. So I'd move toward the children's clinic, which is hands-on, and I'd be the one who sets up the AI for everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set the clinic up so the AI handles the simple online requests completely, with me checking a sample each day. I'd do a course in child development and child safety, because the kids' clinic is the work that lasts. And I'd keep the evening shifts going while they last, because they're also online work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a little uneasy. I can see where to step, I just have to step quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the evening shifts are also online work. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, those are the first to go in this picture, probably within a year or two. I'd treat them as temporary money and not count on them. Sam's ward job is hands-on, so that's our steadier income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the clinic would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The doctors who only want to do online work because it fits around their kids. One colleague does three days a week, all online, from home. In this picture her job shrinks first. I'd feel guilty setting up the system that shrinks my colleague's job.

steps.text: Set up AI to answer the clinic's simple online requests

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast, and I'd be honest that even people like me who like the tools are scared. At work I'd say we need a plan this month, not next year. Online I'd probably go quiet, because I wouldn't know what to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my income takes a big hit by 2028. The thinking work goes, and I'd be left with the children's clinic until robots come around 2031. Sam's ward work is hands-on, so Sam would probably be earning more than me for a few years, which is fine, but we can't live on one wage with this rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for clinical reviewer jobs with the companies building health AI, because someone has to check what the systems do with children. I'd stop the evening shifts, which would be gone anyway, and move every spare bit of money into savings. If it came to it, we'd move somewhere cheaper, maybe near Sam's parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, properly anxious. I like change, but AGI by 2028 is change with a stopwatch on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we need to sit down with the bank app and work out what we can live on. Sam would make tea and say we've got each other, which is true but doesn't pay rent. Then we'd make a list, because that's what we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've spoken about the AI companies. Would you really work for one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if it meant children's care was checked by a doctor. Better me than nobody. I'd want a clear contract about what I'm checking, though, not just to be a name on a form.

feel: Properly **anxious**: change with a stopwatch on it.

fieldNote: Her adaptability doesn't remove fear; she calls it **change with a stopwatch**.
Her partner's **hands-on nursing** would out-earn her for a few years.

steps.text: Apply for clinical reviewer jobs at health AI companies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it if we start now. At the working group I'd propose a plan for which jobs change when. Online I'd share practical stuff for other doctors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years lets me build two things: a specialty in children's health, and a skill in checking AI. By 2031 the thinking work goes, but someone has to oversee AI for children's care, and I'd want that to be me. The hands-on kids' clinic carries on until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a diploma in child health over the next two years, paid monthly. I'd join a national group on AI safety for children's care. And Sam and I would build three months of savings by 2029, which means no holiday for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still nervous, but excited too. I feel like I'd have a real shot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: No holiday for two years. How would Sam take that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam would want one long weekend at least, and we'd compromise on a cheap one. Sam's always been better than me at saying we need a break. I'd probably give in by the second summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after 2034, when robots come for hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. I'd hope the oversight role is still there, because someone answers for what happens to children. But I can't promise myself that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, if people use it, and I'd be fairly upbeat. At the clinic I'd say let's plan calmly. Online I'd write about how doctors can prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well here. I'd have the child health diploma, years running AI at the clinic, and maybe a lead role in children's care for the area. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking work goes and forty when robots arrive, which is a good age to change direction if I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the child health diploma in the first two years and then aim for a lead role. I'd start putting a small amount every month into a pension and an index fund, once we have three months saved. Sam and I would get married in a couple of years, which we've been putting off for money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit uneasy. It's the picture I'd choose if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would ten years make you go ahead with the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it feels like there's a future to plan around. In the fast one, I wouldn't spend a penny on a party. With ten years, a small wedding at Sam's parents' place feels sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you worried about anyone else in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger brother, who's starting a law degree. Law is almost all thinking work, so ten years is exactly when he'd be getting going. I'd tell him to pick something with a hands-on side, or at least to learn the AI from day one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my online half disappears straight away and we've got no savings after the move. What would help is the health service paying doctors to train in AI oversight, rather than us doing it on evenings. And some protection for rent if hours drop suddenly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the parents. A lot of my worried first-time parents already ask an AI chatbot at three in the morning, and then they come to me to check. That checking role is real, and it's growing.

headlineQuote: A lot of my worried first-time parents already ask an AI chatbot at three in the morning, and then they come to me to check.
portrait: Tara is a **27-year-old** doctor at a big clinic on a new estate, splitting online work and a children's clinic.
She uses AI **every day**, sits on the digital working group, and built an inbox sorting tool.
She lives with **Sam**, a children's nurse, and the move emptied their savings.
She sees her **online half** going first and plans to move toward children's health.
With ten years she'd lead children's care and **finally marry** Sam.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her **online work** goes at once and they have **no savings** after the move.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **training** in AI oversight and some **rent protection** if hours drop suddenly.
